questions.question: Which description fits a relaxation of an optimization problem?
options: Keep the constraints; replace the objective by a simpler one.
Keep the objective; add constraints to make the problem smaller.
Keep the objective; remove or weaken some of the constraints.
Remove or weaken constraints and also change the objective.

questions.question: Let $F$ be the feasible set of an optimization problem and $F_R$ the feasible set of a relaxation of it. What does the relation $F\subseteq F_R$ say?
options: Every plan feasible for the original problem is feasible for the relaxation.
The relaxation always has plans that the original problem does not allow.
The original problem and the relaxation have exactly the same feasible plans.
No plan is feasible for both the original problem and the relaxation.

questions.question: A maximization problem and a relaxation of it both have optimal solutions. How does the relaxed optimal value compare with the original optimal value?
options: It is at least the original optimal value.
It is at most the original optimal value.
It is exactly the original optimal value.
It is strictly above the original optimal value.

questions.question: A maximization LP has the finite optimal value 50. A relaxation of it, obtained by dropping two constraints, turns out to have an objective that can be increased without limit. What does this show?
options: The original LP is unbounded as well, since the two problems share one objective.
The relaxation was formed wrongly, since relaxing a bounded problem keeps it bounded.
The relaxation gives no useful benchmark here, and the original optimum stays 50.
The original LP must be infeasible, since its optimum cannot match an unbounded one.

questions.question: A planner already has a feasible plan, found by a simple rule of thumb, for a hard production problem. Why might the planner also solve a relaxation of that problem?
options: It always returns a plan that satisfies every one of the original constraints.
It gives the exact optimal value of the original problem in all cases.
It replaces the original model, whose constraints were unrealistic.
Its optimal value is a benchmark, possibly unattainable, for judging the plan.

questions.question: An LP maximizes $x_1+x_2$ subject to $x_1\le3$, $x_2\le4$, $x_1+x_2\le6$ and $x_1,x_2\ge0$. Which change produces a relaxation of this LP?
options: Add the constraint $x_1\ge1$ as well
Replace $x_1+x_2\le6$ by $x_1+x_2\le5$
Replace the objective by $2x_1+x_2$
Delete the constraint $x_1+x_2\le6$

questions.question: An LP maximizes $x_1+x_2$ subject to $x_1\le3$, $x_2\le4$, $x_1+x_2\le6$ and $x_1,x_2\ge0$; its optimal value is 6. The constraint $x_1+x_2\le6$ is weakened to $x_1+x_2\le8$. What is the optimal value of this relaxation?
options: 7, attained at $(3,4)$
6, attained at $(2,4)$
8, attained at $(4,4)$
5, attained at $(1,4)$

questions.question: Giapetto maximizes $4x_s+x_t$ subject to $2x_s+x_t\le100$, $x_s+x_t\le80$, $x_s\le40$ and $x_s,x_t\ge0$; the optimum is $(40,20)$ with value 180. The constraint $x_s\le40$ is dropped. What is the optimum of this relaxation?
options: $(40,20)$ with value 180
$(50,0)$ with value 200
$(20,60)$ with value 140
$(60,0)$ with value 240

questions.question: An LP maximizes $3x_1+2x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\le5$, $x_1\le3$, $x_2\le4$, $x_1+2x_2\le8$ and $x_1,x_2\ge0$. Dropping $x_1+2x_2\le8$ gives a relaxation whose optimum is $(3,2)$ with value 13. What follows for the original LP?
options: Its optimal value is strictly below 13.
It must be re-solved to find its optimum.
$(3,2)$ is infeasible for it, so 13 is out of reach.
$(3,2)$ is optimal for it, with value 13.

questions.question: A minimization problem has optimal cost 50. A relaxation of it is solved. Which of these could be the optimal cost of the relaxation?
A maximization problem is relaxed, and the relaxed optimizer violates one of the dropped constraints. Must the original optimal value be strictly smaller than the relaxed optimal value?
options: Yes; an infeasible optimizer forces a strict gap.
No; the two optimal values can still be equal.
Yes, unless the dropped constraint is an equation.
No; the original value is then larger.

questions.question: After some constraints of a model are removed, the resulting relaxation turns out to have no feasible solution at all. What does this imply for the original model?
options: It can still be feasible, because its extra constraints restore feasibility.
It is infeasible as well, since its feasible set lies inside the relaxed one.
It must be unbounded, since the relaxation has lost all of its feasible plans.
It is feasible exactly when the removed constraints are satisfied by zero.

questions.question: Why is the optimal value of a relaxation of a maximization problem never below the original optimal value?
options: An original optimal plan stays feasible in the relaxation, with equal value.
The relaxation uses a larger objective function, so all of its values go up.
Both problems always share the same optimal plan, so their values coincide.
Removing constraints raises the objective value of every individual plan.

questions.question: A model minimizes $2x_1+3x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\ge4$, $x_1\le2$ and $x_1,x_2\ge0$; its optimum is $(2,2)$ with cost 10. What is the optimal cost after dropping $x_1\le2$?
For a cost-minimization model, a quick rule finds a feasible plan costing 130. A relaxation of the model has optimal cost 118. Where does the optimal cost of the original model lie?
options: Between 0 and 118, both included
Exactly at 118, the relaxed optimum
Between 118 and 130, both included
Exactly at 130, the found plan's cost

questions.question: An LP maximizes $x_1+x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\le4$, $x_1\le1$ and $x_1,x_2\ge0$. After dropping $x_1\le1$, a solver reports the relaxed optimizer $(4,0)$ with value 4. What is the optimal value of the original LP?
options: 3, attained for example at $(1,2)$
1, attained for example at $(1,0)$
5, attained for example at $(1,4)$
4, attained for example at $(1,3)$

questions.question: A constraint is dropped from a model, and the relaxed optimum happens to satisfy it, so it is optimal for the original model too. An analyst concludes that the constraint can be deleted from the model for good. Is this justified?
options: Partly: it leaves this optimum unchanged but may still exclude other plans.
Yes: as the relaxed optimum satisfies it, the constraint excludes no plans.
No: a relaxed optimum is never optimal for the original model.
No: the original optimal value must be strictly below the relaxed one.

questions.question: A maximization problem $P$ has optimal value $z^*$. Relaxation $R_1$ drops constraint $A$; relaxation $R_2$ drops both $A$ and another constraint $B$. Their optimal values are $z_1$ and $z_2$. Which statement holds?
options: $z^*\le z_2\le z_1$, as dropping $B$ too can only lower the best value
$z_1=z_2$, since both problems are relaxations of the same problem $P$
$z^*\le z_1\le z_2$, so $z_1$ is never further away from $z^*$ than $z_2$
$z_1\le z^*\le z_2$, since only $R_2$ is a relaxation of the problem $P$

questions.question: A model maximizes $x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\le6$, $x_1\le4$ and $x_1,x_2\ge0$. An analyst replaces $x_1+x_2\le6$ by the weaker $x_1+x_2\le8$ but also adds $x_2\le2$, finds the new optimal value 2, and concludes that the original optimum is at most 2. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: weakening $x_1+x_2\le6$ to $x_1+x_2\le8$ makes it a relaxation.
The new right-hand side 8 is too large for a useful relaxation.
Nothing: the objective $x_2$ is kept, which is all a relaxation requires.
The added $x_2\le2$ cuts off original plans such as $(0,6)$ with value 6.

questions.question: For a profit-maximization model, a quick rule finds a feasible plan with profit 200. A relaxation of the model also has optimal value 200, but its reported optimizer violates one of the dropped constraints. What can be concluded about the quick-rule plan?
options: Nothing, since the relaxed optimizer is infeasible for the model.
It is optimal, since no feasible plan can earn more than 200.
It is suboptimal, since the original optimum must exceed 200.
It is optimal only if it equals the reported relaxed optimizer.
